item.title: Overview of 400 Silent Years between the Old and New Testaments - Silence is not Absent 🟢 NEW
item.description: Adapted from insights by Ray C. Stedman and other biblical reflections. Introduction # Imagine walking into a bustling theatre right at intermission. When the first act ended, the stage was small, quiet, and relatively simple. A struggling community of Jewish exiles had just returned to their ancestral homeland in Palestine after seventy years of Babylonian captivity. Living under the tolerant oversight of the Persian Empire, they had rebuilt a modest temple in Jerusalem, far smaller and less dazzling than Solomon’s original masterpiece, yet functional and sacred. Inside its courts, priests tracing an unbroken lineage all the way back to Aaron carried out the daily sacrifices commanded by Moses. Although no descendant of King David wore a crown, Zerubbabel, the rightful royal heir, served merely as a Persian-appointed governor, the people were largely united. There were no rival religious sects, no competing temples, and no foreign legions marching down their cobblestone streets. Yet even after returning from exile, the people’s hearts had once again begun to drift from wholehearted devotion to God. Around 435 BC, the prophet Malachi called Israel to repentance and closed the Old Testament not on a note of defeat or despair, but of expectation, leaving behind a promise that God would one day send His messenger to prepare the way before Him (Malachi 3:1, NIV). Then, the curtain fell.
